title: An Optimal Algorithm for Sorting Pattern-Avoiding Sequences
authors: Michal Opler (Czech Technical University in Prague, Czechia)
abstract: We present a deterministic comparison-based algorithm that sorts sequences avoiding a fixed permutation $\pi$ in linear time, even if $\pi$ is a priori unkown. Moreover, the dependence of the multiplicative constant on the pattern $\pi$ matches the information-theoretic lower bound. A crucial ingredient is an algorithm for performing efficient multi-way merge based on the Marcus-Tardos theorem. As a direct corollary, we obtain a linear-time algorithm for sorting permutations of bounded twin-width.

Abstract—We present a deterministic comparison-based
algorithm that sorts sequences avoiding a fixed permutation
π in linear time, even if π is a priori unkown. Moreover, the
dependence of the multiplicative constant on the pattern π
matches the information-theoretic lower bound. A crucial
ingredient is an algorithm for performing efficient multi-way
merge based on the Marcus-Tardos theorem. As a direct
corollary, we obtain a linear-time algorithm for sorting
permutations of bounded twin-width.

I. I NTRODUCTION
The information-theoretic lower bound on sorting states
that any comparison-based sorting algorithm must take
Ω(n log n) time in the worst case for sorting inputs
of length n, see [10]. Naturally, it invites the question
about complexity of sorting restricted sets of inputs, and
this problem has indeed been studied for decades. In
this paper, we resolve the complexity of sorting input
sequences restricted by avoiding a fixed permutation
pattern.
We distinguish between arbitrary sequences and permutations that contain no repeated values. A sequence
S = s1 , . . . , sn contains a permutation π = π1 , . . . , πk
if there are indices i1 < · · · < ik such that sij < siℓ if
and only if πj < πℓ for all j, ℓ ∈ [k]. We say that the
subsequence si1 , . . . , sik of S is order-isomorphic to π.
Otherwise, S avoids π.
Lower bounds: A standard argument shows that
any comparison-based algorithm for sorting a set of
permutations Γ , each of length n, must make at least
Ω(log |Γ | + n) comparisons in the worst case. Fredman [13] showed that O(log |Γ | + n) comparisons
suffice if we have complete knowledge of Γ and unrestricted computational power. Specifically, Fredman’s
argument proves the existence of a decision tree of
depth O(log |Γ | + n) that correctly sorts Γ . In order
to apply these bounds on pattern-avoiding sequences, it
invites the natural question of how many pattern-avoiding
permutations of given length are there. In fact, it has been
a long-standing open problem in the world of patternavoiding permutations whether the number of π-avoiding

Pattern-agnostic algorithms: However, a completely
different approach proved lately fruitful. Instead of
designing a specific algorithm depending on the avoided
pattern, a general-purpose sorting algorithm is used, and
the pattern-avoidance appears merely in the analysis of
its runtime. This approach offers two main advantages
over pattern-specific algorithms – it covers all choices of
the avoided pattern π simultaneously and moreover, the
runtime on a specific input is bounded by the patterns it
avoids even though the algorithm itself has no knowledge
of them.
Chalermsook, Goswami, Kozma, Mehlhorn, and Saranurak [6] were the first to consider this approach with
their focus being on binary search trees (BSTs). They
analyzed the performance of an online BST balancing
strategy G REEDY F UTURE [11] and showed that with its
O(k)
use a π-avoiding sequence can be sorted in 2α(n)
·n
time where k is the length of π and α(·) is the inverseAckermann function. Later, Kozma and Saranurak [19]
introduced a new heap data structure S MOOTH H EAP and
showed that a heap sort with S MOOTH H EAP reaches the
same asymptotic bound on runtime while being much
easier to implement than G REEDY F UTURE. Recently, the
bound on sorting with G REEDY F UTURE was improved

to 2O(k )+(1+o(1))α(n) · n by Chalermsook, Pettie and
Yingchareonthawornchai [8]. Tighter bounds on sorting
with G REEDY F UTURE are known only for specific sets of
inputs such as O(nk 2 ) for (k, . . . , 1)-avoiding permutations [7] or O(n log k) for the so-called k-decomposable
permutations [15].
BSTs and dynamic optimality: Arguably, the most
famous open question related to sorting is the dynamic
optimality conjecture [22] asking whether the splay tree is
an instance-optimal online BST balancing strategy. More
recently, the conjecture is usually rephrased as asking
whether there exists any instance-optimal online BST
strategy with G REEDY F UTURE being the other prime
candidate alongside splay trees. Observe that any instanceoptimal balancing strategy must also work within the
bounds proved for G REEDY F UTURE [6], [7], [8] and thus,
any such strategy can be used to sort pattern-avoiding
sequences in near-linear time. However, none of these
results implies that an instance-optimal BST strategy must
sort pattern-avoiding sequences in linear time, and it has
been raised as an open question [6] whether this is, in fact,
a corollary of dynamic optimality. Berendsohn, Kozma
and Opler [3] resolved this question positively by showing

that any instance-optimal BST balancing strategy sorts
π-avoiding sequences in time O(c2π n). They construct an
offline sequence of BST modifications that accommodates
a given π-avoiding input with linear cost. However, an
Ω(n log n) time is still needed for the computation of
this sequence and therefore, this result in itself does not
imply the existence of a linear-time algorithm for sorting
pattern-avoiding sequences.
Twin-width: Lastly, there is a close connection
between pattern avoidance and the recently emerging
notion of twin-width. Without going into too much
detail, twin-width is a structural parameter introduced
for permutations by Guillemot and Marx [16], and later
extended to graphs and arbitrary relational structures by
Bonnet, Kim, Thomassé and Watrigant [5]. Guillemot
and Marx [16] showed that the twin-width of any πavoiding permutation is at most O(cπ ) and conversely,
any permutation of twin-width d avoids a certain pattern
π with cπ = 2O(d) . As a result, bounded twin-width can
been exploited to prove properties of pattern-avoiding
permutations and sequences [4], [3].
A. Our result
Our main result is an asymptotically optimal sorting
algorithm for pattern-avoiding sequences that matches
the information-theoretic lower bound for each π up to
a global constant.
Theorem I.1. There is an algorithm that sorts a πavoiding sequence S of length n in O((log cπ + 1) · n)
time even if π is a priori unknown.
The algorithm is built from two components. The first
one is an efficient multi-way merge procedure capable of
merging up to logn n sequences with n elements in total,
as long as the sequences originate from a π-avoiding
input. Its analysis is heavily based on the Marcus-Tardos
theorem [20].
The second component is an efficient algorithm to
sort a large set of short sequences. Naturally, many sequences in such a set must be pairwise order-isomorphic,
which suggests that we could try grouping them into
equivalence classes and then actually sorting only one
sequence from each class. Unfortunately, computing the
equivalence classes is in some sense as hard as sorting
itself. Instead, we take a different approach of guessing a
shallow decision tree for sorting π-avoiding permutations
guaranteed by the result of Fredman [13].
Theorem I.1 follows by first cutting up the input into
sequences of length roughly log log log n which we can
efficiently sort using the optimal decision tree. The sorted
sequences then serve as a basis for a bottom-up merge
sort using the efficient multi-way merge.
Furthermore, let us point out that Theorem I.1 achieves
the information-theoretic lower bound for arbitrary π-

Structure of the paper: In Section II, we introduce
the necessary notions and review relevant facts about the
Füredi-Hajnal limits. An efficient algorithm for multiway merging is presented in Section III, followed by an
efficient algorithm for sorting a large number of short
sequences in Section IV. Finally, Theorem I.1 is proved

Recall that there is a connection between patternavoiding permutations and permutations of bounded twinwidth. In particular, any permutation of twin-width d
avoids a certain pattern π, the so-called d × d-grid
with Füredi-Hajnal limit cπ ∈ 2O(d) . It follows that
the algorithm of Theorem I.1 can also be used to
sort permutations of bounded twin-width in linear time,
without having access to a decomposition of small width.

II. P RELIMINARIES
Permutations and avoidance: A permutation π of
length n is a sequence π1 , . . . , πn in which each number
from the set [n] = {1, . . . , n} appears exactly once.
Alternatively, we can represent π as an n × n binary
permutation matrix Mπ where the cell in the ith column
and jth row, denoted Mπ (i, j), contains a 1-entry if
and only if j = πi . Note that for consistency with
permutations, we number rows of matrices bottom to
top. A permutation sequence is any sequence s1 , . . . , sn
of pairwise distinct values. We say that two sequences
(not necessarily permutations) s1 , . . . , sn and t1 , . . . , tn
are order-isomorphic if for each i, j ∈ [n], we have
si < sj if and only if ti < tj . We say that a sequence S
contains a permutation π if some subsequence of S is
order-isomorphic to π. Otherwise, we say that S avoids π.
See Figure 1.
Additionally, we define avoidance for binary matrices.
We say that a binary matrix M contains a binary matrix
P if P can be obtained from M by deleting rows or
columns and changing an arbitrary subset of 1-entries to
zero. Otherwise, M avoids P .
Furedi Hajnal limits: For a permutation π, let
exπ (n) denote the maximum number of 1-entries in a
π-avoiding n × n binary matrix. The celebrated MarcusTardos theorem [20], previously known as the FürediHajnal conjecture, states that exπ (n) is at most O(n) for
each fixed π. It was observed by Cibulka [9] that the
limit cπ = limn→∞ n1 exπ (n) exists. This limit is known
as the Füredi-Hajnal limit of π. Furthermore, we have
exπ (n) ≤ cπ · n for all n due to the superadditivity of
exπ (·) [9], which easily extends to rectangular matrices.

Corollary I.2. There is a comparison-based algorithm
that sorts a permutation of length n and twin-with d in
O(d · n) time even if d is a priori unknown.
Guillemot and Marx [16] devised a fixed-parameter
tractable (fpt-) algorithm that computes a twin-width
decomposition of width 2O(d) for any permutation τ
of twin-width d and length n in O(n) time. Crucially,
their algorithm assumes access to τ in sorted order
by values, and otherwise its running time degrades
to O(n log n) due to the extra sorting step. However,
Corollary I.2 speeds up the sorting step to linear time,
and thus a 2O(d) -wide decomposition can be computed
in O(d · n) time even in the comparison-based model. As
a consequence, the running time of several fpt-algorithms
can be improved from Od (n log n) to Od (n) when the
input permutation of twin-width d is given as a comparison oracle without any precomputed decomposition.
This improvement concerns (i) the permutation pattern
matching algorithm by Guillemot and Marx [16], (ii) the
algorithm for first-order model checking by Bonnet,
Kim, Thomassé and Watrigant [5], (iii) the algorithm for
factoring pattern-avoiding permutations into separable
ones by Bonnet, Bourneuf, Geniet and Thomassé [4],
and (iv) algorithms for various optimization problems
on pattern-avoiding inputs by Berendsohn, Kozma and
Opler [3].

B. Without prior knowledge of π
Now, we consider the more general case where π (and
cπ in particular) is not known to the algorithm. However,
we still restrict inputs to permutation sequences. The
basic idea is to guess cπ by starting with a constant,
trying the previous approach for a bounded number of

Description of the algorithm: Initially, we set d = 1
and the algorithm proceeds in phases until all the elements

the phase was odd, we perform one additional merge to
ensure that we always decrease the number of sequences
by at least half. Let us denote by di the value of d in the
ith phase. It follows that in the ith phase, we work with
mi ≤ 2mi sequences and di is equal to 2i . In particular,

Afterwards, the algorithm follows the case where cπ
was known, i.e. it proceeds in rounds where in each

A standard binary heap is again used for efficiently

It is important that whenever a new phase begins,
the algorithm does not reset to the very beginning as
there is no reason to do so. The output to this point
is a valid prefix of the sorted sequence. Thus, the next
phase continues with only the remaining elements in each
sequence.
As before, the algorithm clearly outputs a correctly
sorted sequence, and it only remains to bound its running
time.
